  <div class="eyebrow page-eyebrow">Customer Analytics · Case Study</div>
  <h1 class="page-title">Arithmetic before algorithms</h1>
  <p class="article-deck">
    I worked the same direct-mail campaign twice. The first pass was about getting the
    economics right, and hid a <em>24-fold</em> error in a summary table. The second threw seven models
    at it and found that the best one beat plain logistic regression by <em>0.7%</em>. Put together,
    they say something uncomfortable about where analytical effort actually pays.
  </p>

  <dl class="article-meta">
    <div><dt>Role</dt><dd>Analyst</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Case</dt><dd>Direct-mail upgrade campaign, two passes</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Stack</dt><dd>Python · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn · XGBoost</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Course</dt><dd>MGTA 455, Rady School of Management</dd></div>
  </dl>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The campaign</h2>
    <p>An accounting-software company mailed an upgrade offer to its small-business customers.
    <strong>801,821</strong> businesses received wave one; <strong>38,487</strong> bought — a 4.8%
    response. That leaves <strong>763,334</strong> who didn't, and the question is which of them are
    worth a second stamp.</p>
    <p>The unit economics fit in a sentence. A mailing costs <strong>$1.41</strong>. An upgrade earns
    <strong>$60</strong> in margin. Mailing someone pays off when their response probability clears
    $1.41 ÷ $60 — a breakeven of <strong>2.35%</strong>.</p>
    <p>Except wave two won't perform like wave one. These are, by definition, people who already said
    no once, and the working assumption is that they respond at <strong>half</strong> the rate. That
    one assumption is where the first pass got interesting.</p>
  </section>

  <hr class="article-rule">

  <section class="article-section">
    <div class="article-part"><span class="article-part-n">1</span><span class="article-part-l">First pass · the economics</span></div>
    <h2>Where the 50% goes — twice</h2>
    <p>The halving does two different jobs, and they are easy to conflate.</p>
    <p><strong>Job one: it raises the bar for who gets mailed.</strong> If a customer's wave-one score
    is 4%, their wave-two probability is really 2% — below breakeven. So the threshold on the wave-one
    score doubles, from 2.35% to <strong>4.70%</strong>.</p>
    <p><strong>Job two: it shrinks the revenue you book from the people you did mail.</strong> Someone
    scored at 10% in wave one is expected to convert at 5%. Their expected revenue is 0.05 × $60, not
    0.10 × $60.</p>
    <p>Do only the first and the mailing list is right while every profit figure is roughly double what
    it should be. Do only the second and you mail thousands of people who can't pay their way.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-title">Is this customer worth a $1.41 stamp?</div>
    <div class="article-panel-sub">Set a wave-one predicted response rate and follow the arithmetic through
    both applications of the 50% decay.</div>
    <div class="article-calc-grid">
      <div>
        <div class="article-slider-row">
          <span class="article-slider-lab">Wave-one predicted response</span>
          <span class="article-slider-val" id="pv">8.69%</span>
        </div>
        <input type="range" id="p" min="0" max="200" value="87" step="1"
               aria-label="Wave-one predicted response rate, percent">
        <div class="article-ticks"><span>0%</span><span>5%</span><span>10%</span><span>15%</span><span>20%</span></div>
        <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>
      </div>
      <div class="ledger" id="ledger"></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Applying that rule to a held-out test set of 22,500 customers, with a logistic model built on
    demographics, purchase history and geography:</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-title">Wave-two economics on the held-out test set</div>
    <div class="article-panel-sub">Each step is the previous one after one filter or one multiplication.</div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="funnel" viewBox="0 0 720 300" role="img"
        aria-label="Funnel from 22,500 test customers to 9,957 dollars of expected profit"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tipf"></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">8,322</div><div class="article-stat-l">Mailed, of 22,500</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$1.20</div><div class="article-stat-l">Profit per letter</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0.85</div><div class="article-stat-l">Return on marketing expense</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$9,957</div><div class="article-stat-l">Expected test-set profit</div></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>About <strong>37%</strong> of non-responders clear the bar, and each letter returns roughly
    <strong>$1.20</strong> against its $1.41 cost — 85 cents of profit per dollar of postage. The model
    held its shape out of sample: $1.1588 per letter on training against $1.1965 on test.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The error I didn't catch</h2>
    <div class="article-flagbox">
      <p>The detailed work put the logistic model at about <strong>$1.20 of profit per mailed
      customer</strong>. A summary table at the end of the same notebook, using the same model and the
      same 4.70% threshold, implies about <strong>$28.47 per customer</strong> — roughly 24 times
      higher.</p>
      <p>That figure can't be right, and it's checkable without rerunning anything. Profit per letter
      is (p × 0.5 × $60) − $1.41. For that to reach $28.47, the average response probability would have
      to be about <strong>99%</strong>. The predictions in the data sit between 2% and 18%. Somewhere
      between the two calculations a column is being read on the wrong scale.</p>
    </div>
    <p>The lesson is about bounds. Profit per letter here has a hard ceiling of
    <strong>$28.59</strong> — half of $60, less the stamp. Any result brushing against a ceiling like
    that is telling you something has gone wrong. I had the bound available the whole time and never
    checked the summary against it.</p>
    <p>Which is what sent me back for a second pass — this time asking a different question.</p>
  </section>

  <hr class="article-rule">

  <section class="article-section">
    <div class="article-part"><span class="article-part-n">2</span><span class="article-part-l">Second pass · the models</span></div>
    <h2>Is a better model worth anything here?</h2>
    <p>The economics were now settled. What remained was a narrower question: <em>how much profit is
    left on the table by a model simple enough to explain to a marketing director?</em></p>
    <p>So I rebuilt the analysis with seven scoring models on the same features and the same split —
    three families, tuned and untuned — judged on the only thing that matters, which is dollars on a
    held-out test set.</p>
    <p>The rebuild also settled the earlier discrepancy. Running the same decision-list formula in the
    new pipeline produced about <strong>$2.12 per letter</strong> — a plausible figure, comfortably
    under the $28.59 ceiling. That confirms the $28.47 was a scaling fault in the first notebook's
    prediction columns rather than anything wrong with the formula itself.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Ranking quality against money earned</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">Test-set AUC on the horizontal axis, expected test-set profit on the
        vertical. Hover any model for its full numbers.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-legend">
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw article-sw-r" style="background:var(--s-1)"></span>Logistic</div>
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw article-sw-r" style="background:var(--s-2)"></span>Neural network</div>
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw article-sw-r" style="background:var(--s-3)"></span>Tree ensemble</div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="scatter" viewBox="0 0 720 400" role="img"
        aria-label="Scatter plot of test AUC against test profit for seven models"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip1"></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Four models cluster tightly in the top right — tuned XGBoost, logistic regression and both
    neural networks land between <strong>$12,914</strong> and <strong>$13,249</strong>, with AUCs
    within 0.0015 of each other. Three tree models trail well behind.</p>
    <p>Best result: tuned XGBoost at <strong>$13,249.17</strong>. Logistic regression:
    <strong>$13,153.20</strong>. A difference of <strong>$95.97</strong>, or <strong>0.7%</strong>.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$95.97</div><div class="article-stat-l">XGBoost's edge on the test set</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0.0009</div><div class="article-stat-l">Its edge in AUC</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$3,424</div><div class="article-stat-l">Edge scaled to 763,334 letters</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0.7%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Of campaign profit</div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Expected campaign profit, full population</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">The dashed line marks plain logistic regression. Everything to its
        right is what additional model complexity bought.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="article-seg" role="group" aria-label="Scale">
        <button id="b-full" aria-pressed="true">Full population</button>
        <button id="b-test" aria-pressed="false">Test set</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="ladder" viewBox="0 0 720 340" role="img"
        aria-label="Horizontal bar chart of expected campaign profit by model"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip2"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
      <table class="article-table">
        <thead><tr><th>Model</th><th>Test AUC</th><th>Mailed</th><th>Test profit</th><th>Full population</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody id="tbody"></tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>Random forest mailed <strong>more</strong> customers than any other model — 6,569 — and earned
      the <strong>least</strong>, at $343,824. Volume isn't the win. Getting the order right at the top
      of the list is, because everyone near the 4.70% line contributes almost nothing either way.</p>
    </div>
    <p>The spread that matters isn't first versus second. It's the leading cluster versus the trailing
    one: tuned XGBoost beats plain random forest by <strong>$128,838</strong>, or 37%. Choosing a
    <em>bad</em> model is expensive. Choosing among good ones is nearly free.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Where AUC and profit disagree</h2>
    <p>The two rankings mostly track each other, and then they don't. The untuned neural network posts
    a higher AUC than logistic regression — 0.7663 against 0.7661 — but earns <strong>$239
    less</strong>. Tuning it <em>lowered</em> its AUC to 0.7655 while <em>raising</em> its profit to
    $12,956.</p>
    <p>That's a mismatch of objectives rather than noise. AUC integrates ranking quality across the
    whole list, including the vast middle where nobody gets mailed. Profit depends only on who lands
    above 4.70% and how those particular customers are ordered. A model can improve its handling of
    the bottom half — which AUC rewards — while getting slightly worse at the only region that pays.</p>
    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>If the decision is a threshold, evaluate at the threshold. AUC is a reasonable model-selection
      heuristic and a poor final arbiter.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The technical layer</h2>
    <div class="article-tech-label">For readers who want the mechanics</div>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>The full profit expression</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>For a customer with wave-one predicted probability <em>p</em>, mailed in wave two:</p>
    <p><strong>expected profit = (p × 0.5 × $60) − $1.41</strong></p>
    <p>Setting that to zero gives p = 1.41 ÷ 30 = 0.047. The same threshold arrives from either
    direction: halve the response and compare to the $60 margin, or leave the response alone and compare
    to a doubled breakeven. What you cannot do is take the doubled threshold as permission to skip the
    halving in the revenue term — that is the double-count.</p>
    <p>Aggregating over the mailed set in the first pass: 8,322 letters at $1.41 is $11,734.02 of cost.
    The summed half-rate probabilities give 361.52 expected responders, worth $21,691.41 at $60 each.
    The difference, $9,957.39, is the expected profit — and ROME is that divided by cost, 0.8486.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Scaling a test-set result to the real population</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>The 75,000-record dataset is a sample; the actual wave-two audience is 801,821 − 38,487 =
    <strong>763,334</strong> businesses. Extrapolating multiplies test-set profit by the ratio of the
    real eligible population to the eligible test sample.</p>
    <p>Two conditions must hold. The test sample has to be representative, and the filter must match on
    both sides — the test set is restricted to wave-one non-responders, so the population figure has to
    exclude the 38,487 responders too. Both passes handle that correctly.</p>
    <p>What extrapolation cannot do is manufacture precision. A per-letter error of a few cents becomes
    tens of thousands of dollars at 763,334 letters. Since every model is scaled by the same constant,
    the full-population column changes the magnitudes but never the ordering.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Why the tree models underperformed</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Random forest and gradient boosting landed at AUCs of 0.71 to 0.73 while the linear and neural
    models reached 0.766 or better — the reverse of what people usually expect from tree ensembles.</p>
    <p>The likely reason is the shape of the problem. Response is rare, signal is weak and spread thin
    across many mildly informative variables, and much of the structure — recency, spend, geography — is
    close to monotone in the log odds. That is a setting linear models handle gracefully. Trees spend
    their capacity looking for interactions, and when the real interactions are few, they mostly find
    noise.</p>
    <p>Tuned XGBoost recovers to 0.7670 because regularization and shallow depth push it back toward
    smoothness. It wins by becoming more like the simple model, not less.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>The geographic features need a stricter construction</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Both passes build a zip-region response feature from observed wave-one response, which lifts AUC
    substantially. The reasoning is that wave one has already happened, so this is information a real
    marketer would have — and that part is sound.</p>
    <p>What matters is <em>which rows</em> the rate is computed from. If a customer's own outcome
    contributes to the average for their zip bin, the feature carries a trace of the answer and test-set
    performance is flattered. The fix is to compute the rate on training rows only and map it onto the
    test set, or to use out-of-fold estimates. I can't tell from the notebooks that this was done, which
    means I can't rule it out — and because every model shares the feature, it would inflate all of them
    rather than change their ordering.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Why response decay is an assumption, not a measurement</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>The 50% figure is given by the case, and everything downstream is proportional to it. If the true
    decay is 40%, breakeven moves to 3.53% and the mailing list grows; at 60%, breakeven rises to 5.88%
    and the list shrinks sharply.</p>
    <p>Because profit per letter is small relative to the $1.41 cost, list size is quite sensitive to
    this one number. A sensitivity analysis across a range of decay assumptions would be more useful to a
    decision-maker than any point estimate, and it costs almost nothing — you already have the scores.</p>
    <p>The cleaner answer is to measure it: hold out a random slice of the wave-two mailing, observe the
    actual decay, and replace the assumption with data before scaling to 763,334.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What a single test set can and cannot settle</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>A $96 gap on roughly 6,300 mailed customers is about 1.5 cents per letter. There is no plausible
    reading of one test split where that difference is real.</p>
    <p>To say anything about first place I would need repeated splits or bootstrapped resamples and a
    distribution of the profit difference. My expectation is that the leading four models would be
    statistically indistinguishable and the tree pair clearly separated — which leaves the interesting
    conclusion intact and the horse race correctly abandoned. The 37% gap between the leading cluster and
    plain random forest is far too large to be sampling noise.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What I'd do differently</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p><strong>Reconcile every summary against its detail.</strong> The 24× discrepancy survived into a
    final table because nothing forced the two calculations to agree. A single assertion that per-letter
    profit stays under $28.59 would have caught it.</p>
    <p><strong>Recompute the zip features out-of-fold.</strong> Cheap, removes the ambiguity, and if the
    AUC gain survives it becomes a much stronger claim.</p>
    <p><strong>Report confidence intervals on the profit differences,</strong> and stop naming a single
    winner when the top four sit inside the noise.</p>
    <p><strong>Select on profit rather than AUC.</strong> Once the decision rule is a threshold,
    cross-validating on expected profit at that threshold aligns model selection with the objective.</p>
    <p><strong>Add cost of ownership to the comparison.</strong> The full-population gap between XGBoost
    and logistic regression is $3,424 a campaign — which does not obviously cover retuning, monitoring
    and explaining a boosted ensemble to a marketing team, when the logistic model hands you coefficients
    that make the targeting rule legible to the people who approve it.</p>
    </div>
    </details>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What this case taught me</h2>
    <p>Two passes at one campaign, and the comparison between them is the actual finding.</p>
    <p><strong>The arithmetic error was worth 24×. The model choice was worth 0.7%.</strong> One of those
    came from an assumption applied in the wrong number of places; the other from weeks of tuning across
    three model families. They are not remotely the same size, and the smaller one is the one that feels
    like real work.</p>
    <p><strong>An assumption that appears twice has to be applied twice.</strong> The 50% decay is one
    belief about the world doing two separate jobs — deciding who is worth mailing, and deciding what
    their response is worth. Handling it once in a two-place problem produces confident, plausible,
    wrong numbers.</p>
    <p><strong>Most arithmetic errors are catchable with a bound.</strong> Profit per letter cannot exceed
    $28.59 here. Probabilities cannot exceed one. Knowing the ceiling on a number is the fastest way to
    notice when a calculation has quietly stopped making sense — faster, and cheaper, than any amount of
    model selection.</p>
    <div class="chips article-chips">
      <span class="chip">Direct-marketing economics</span>
      <span class="chip">Breakeven analysis</span>
      <span class="chip">Profit-based evaluation</span>
      <span class="chip">Logistic regression</span>
      <span class="chip">XGBoost</span>
      <span class="chip">Random forests</span>
      <span class="chip">Neural networks</span>
      <span class="chip">Leakage diagnosis</span>
      <span class="chip">Population scaling</span>
      <span class="chip">polars</span>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine">Figures are from my own analysis on the course dataset. The underlying case materials
    and data are proprietary to the publisher and are not reproduced here.</p>
  </section>
</div>

<script>
  const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(e => { if (e.isIntersecting) e.target.classList.add('visible'); });
  }, { threshold: 0.08 });
  document.querySelectorAll('.reveal').forEach(el => io.observe(el));

  (function(){
    function el(n,a){var e=document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg",n);
      for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}
    function place(tip,host,node){
      var hb=host.getBoundingClientRect(),bb=node.getBoundingClientRect();
      var lx=bb.left-hb.left+bb.width/2-tip.offsetWidth/2;
      tip.style.left=Math.max(4,Math.min(lx,hb.width-tip.offsetWidth-4))+"px";
      tip.style.top=(bb.top-hb.top-tip.offsetHeight-9)+"px";
    }

    (function(){
      var MARGIN=60,COST=1.41,DECAY=0.5,BE=COST/(MARGIN*DECAY);
      var pv=document.getElementById("pv"),sl=document.getElementById("p"),
          led=document.getElementById("ledger"),vd=document.getElementById("verdict");
      function money(v){return (v<0?"−$":"$")+Math.abs(v).toFixed(2);}
      function render(){
        var p=(+sl.value)/10/100, w2=p*DECAY, rev=w2*MARGIN, net=rev-COST;
        pv.textContent=(p*100).toFixed(2)+"%";
        led.innerHTML=
          "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>Wave-one predicted response</span>"+
            "<span class='led-v'>"+(p*100).toFixed(2)+"%</span></div>"+
          "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>× 50% decay → wave-two response</span>"+
            "<span class='led-v'>"+(w2*100).toFixed(2)+"%</span></div>"+
          "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>× $60 margin → expected revenue</span>"+
            "<span class='led-v'>"+money(rev)+"</span></div>"+
          "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>− mailing cost</span>"+
            "<span class='led-v'>−$1.41</span></div>"+
          "<div class='led-row tot'><span>Expected profit per letter</span>"+
            "<span class='led-v'>"+money(net)+"</span></div>";
        var ok=p>BE;
        vd.innerHTML="<span class='badge "+(ok?"yes":"no")+"'>"+(ok?"Mail":"Skip")+"</span><br>"+
          (ok? "Clears the <strong>4.70%</strong> bar. This letter returns <strong>"+money(net)+
               "</strong> above its cost."
             : "Falls below the <strong>4.70%</strong> bar. Mailing loses <strong>"+
               money(Math.abs(net))+"</strong> on this customer.");
      }
      sl.addEventListener("input",render);render();
    })();

    (function(){
      var svg=document.getElementById("funnel"),tip=document.getElementById("tipf"),
          host=svg.parentNode.parentNode;
      var steps=[
        {k:"Test customers",v:"22,500",w:1.00,c:"var(--tan)",ink:"var(--ink)",
         d:"Held-out wave-one non-responders available to score."},
        {k:"Clear 4.70% bar",v:"8,322",w:0.62,c:"var(--s-1)",ink:"#fff",
         d:"37% of the test set. Everyone else costs more to reach than they return."},
        {k:"Expected responders",v:"361.5",w:0.40,c:"var(--s-1)",ink:"#fff",
         d:"Sum of wave-two probabilities — each score halved before adding."},
        {k:"Revenue at $60",v:"$21,691",w:0.40,c:"var(--s-3)",ink:"#fff",
         d:"361.5 responders × $60 margin."},
        {k:"Postage",v:"−$11,734",w:0.22,c:"var(--s-2)",ink:"#fff",
         d:"8,322 letters × $1.41."},
        {k:"Expected profit",v:"$9,957",w:0.18,c:"var(--ink)",ink:"var(--bg)",
         d:"$1.1965 per letter mailed. ROME 0.8486."}
      ];
      var W=720,H=300,ML=132,MR=16,MT=18,MB=16,pw=W-ML-MR,ph=H-MT-MB;
      var rh=ph/steps.length,bh=Math.min(28,rh-8);
      steps.forEach(function(s,i){
        var cy=MT+rh*i+rh/2,bw=Math.max(56,pw*s.w),g=el("g",{});
        var r=el("rect",{x:ML,y:cy-bh/2,width:bw,height:bh,rx:4,fill:s.c});g.appendChild(r);
        var kl=el("text",{x:ML-12,y:cy+4,"text-anchor":"end","class":"article-mlab"});
        kl.textContent=s.k;g.appendChild(kl);
        var vl=el("text",{x:ML+12,y:cy+4,"class":"article-vlab",fill:s.ink});
        vl.textContent=s.v;g.appendChild(vl);
        var hit=el("rect",{x:0,y:cy-rh/2,width:W,height:rh,fill:"transparent"});
        hit.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
          r.setAttribute("opacity",".82");
          tip.innerHTML="<b>"+s.k+" · "+s.v+"</b><br>"+s.d;
          tip.style.opacity=1;place(tip,host,hit);
        });
        hit.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){r.setAttribute("opacity","1");tip.style.opacity=0;});
        g.appendChild(hit);svg.appendChild(g);
      });
    })();

    var M=[
      {k:"XGBoost (tuned)",      f:2, auc:0.7670, mail:6263, t:13249.17, p:472661.68},
      {k:"Logistic regression",  f:0, auc:0.7661, mail:6480, t:13153.20, p:469237.97},
      {k:"Neural net (tuned)",   f:1, auc:0.7655, mail:6492, t:12956.28, p:462212.88},
      {k:"Neural net",           f:1, auc:0.7663, mail:6075, t:12914.25, p:460713.47},
      {k:"Gradient boosting",    f:2, auc:0.7270, mail:5460, t:10961.40, p:391045.91},
      {k:"Random forest (tuned)",f:2, auc:0.7187, mail:6450, t:10465.50, p:373354.77},
      {k:"Random forest",        f:2, auc:0.7099, mail:6569, t: 9637.71, p:343823.51}
    ];
    var FC=["var(--s-1)","var(--s-2)","var(--s-3)"];
    var FN=["Logistic","Neural network","Tree ensemble"];
    function usd(v){return "$"+v.toLocaleString("en-US",{minimumFractionDigits:2,maximumFractionDigits:2});}
    function usd0(v){return "$"+Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US");}

    (function(){
      var svg=document.getElementById("scatter"),tip=document.getElementById("tip1"),
          host=svg.parentNode.parentNode;
      var W=720,H=400,ML=74,MR=118,MT=32,MB=54,pw=W-ML-MR,ph=H-MT-MB;
      var x0=0.700,x1=0.775,y0=9000,y1=13800;
      var X=function(v){return ML+(v-x0)/(x1-x0)*pw;},
          Y=function(v){return MT+ph-(v-y0)/(y1-y0)*ph;};
      for(var t=9000;t<=13500;t+=1500){
        svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:ML,x2:ML+pw,y1:Y(t),y2:Y(t),stroke:"var(--grid)","stroke-width":1}));
        var yl=el("text",{x:ML-10,y:Y(t)+4,"text-anchor":"end","class":"article-ax"});
        yl.textContent="$"+(t/1000).toFixed(1)+"k";svg.appendChild(yl);
      }
      for(var a=0.70;a<=0.7751;a+=0.025){
        var xv=Math.round(a*1000)/1000;
        svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:X(xv),x2:X(xv),y1:MT,y2:MT+ph,stroke:"var(--grid)","stroke-width":1}));
        var xl=el("text",{x:X(xv),y:MT+ph+20,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-ax"});
        xl.textContent=xv.toFixed(3);svg.appendChild(xl);
      }
      var xt=el("text",{x:ML+pw/2,y:MT+ph+42,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-ax"});
      xt.textContent="Test-set AUC →";svg.appendChild(xt);
      var yt=el("text",{x:ML,y:MT-12,"text-anchor":"start","class":"article-ax"});
      yt.textContent="Expected test-set profit";svg.appendChild(yt);
      M.forEach(function(m){
        var cx=X(m.auc),cy=Y(m.t);
        var c=el("circle",{cx:cx,cy:cy,r:8,fill:FC[m.f],stroke:"var(--card)","stroke-width":2});
        svg.appendChild(c);
        var lab=el("text",{x:cx+13,y:cy+4,"class":"article-plab"});
        lab.textContent=m.k;svg.appendChild(lab);
        var hit=el("circle",{cx:cx,cy:cy,r:17,fill:"transparent"});
        hit.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
          c.setAttribute("r",10);
          tip.innerHTML="<b>"+m.k+"</b><br>"+FN[m.f]+"<br>AUC "+m.auc.toFixed(4)+"<br>"+
            m.mail.toLocaleString("en-US")+" mailed<br>"+usd(m.t)+" test profit";
          tip.style.opacity=1;place(tip,host,hit);
        });
        hit.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){c.setAttribute("r",8);tip.style.opacity=0;});
        svg.appendChild(hit);
      });
    })();

    (function(){
      var svg=document.getElementById("ladder"),tip=document.getElementById("tip2"),
          host=svg.parentNode.parentNode,tb=document.getElementById("tbody"),mode="full";
      function draw(){
        while(svg.firstChild)svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
        var W=720,H=340,ML=152,MR=94,MT=22,MB=40,pw=W-ML-MR,ph=H-MT-MB;
        var key=mode==="full"?"p":"t", max=mode==="full"?500000:14000;
        var ref=mode==="full"?469237.97:13153.20, step=mode==="full"?100000:3500;
        var X=function(v){return ML+(v/max)*pw;};
        for(var t=0;t<=max;t+=step){
          svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:X(t),x2:X(t),y1:MT-4,y2:MT+ph,stroke:"var(--grid)","stroke-width":1}));
          var xl=el("text",{x:X(t),y:MT+ph+19,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-ax"});
          xl.textContent=t===0?"$0":"$"+(t/1000).toFixed(0)+"k";svg.appendChild(xl);
        }
        var rh=ph/M.length,bh=Math.min(24,rh-9);
        M.forEach(function(m,i){
          var cy=MT+rh*i+rh/2,v=m[key];
          var bar=el("rect",{x:ML,y:cy-bh/2,width:Math.max(2,X(v)-ML),height:bh,rx:4,fill:FC[m.f]});
          svg.appendChild(bar);
          var kl=el("text",{x:ML-12,y:cy+4,"text-anchor":"end","class":"article-mlab"});
          kl.textContent=m.k;svg.appendChild(kl);
          var vl=el("text",{x:X(v)+9,y:cy+4,"class":"article-vlab"});
          vl.textContent=mode==="full"?usd0(v):usd(v);svg.appendChild(vl);
          var hit=el("rect",{x:0,y:cy-rh/2,width:W,height:rh,fill:"transparent"});
          hit.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
            bar.setAttribute("opacity",".8");
            var d=m.p-469237.97;
            tip.innerHTML="<b>"+m.k+"</b><br>"+m.mail.toLocaleString("en-US")+" mailed · AUC "+
              m.auc.toFixed(4)+"<br>"+usd(m.t)+" test · "+usd0(m.p)+" full<br>"+
              (Math.abs(d)<1?"the logistic benchmark":(d>0?"+":"−")+usd0(Math.abs(d))+" vs logistic");
            tip.style.opacity=1;place(tip,host,hit);
          });
          hit.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){bar.setAttribute("opacity","1");tip.style.opacity=0;});
          svg.appendChild(hit);
        });
        svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:X(ref),x2:X(ref),y1:MT-4,y2:MT+ph,stroke:"var(--ink)",
          "stroke-width":1.5,"stroke-dasharray":"5 4"}));
      }
      tb.innerHTML=M.map(function(m){
        return "<tr"+(m.f===0?" class='hi'":"")+"><td>"+m.k+"</td><td>"+m.auc.toFixed(4)+"</td><td>"+
          m.mail.toLocaleString("en-US")+"</td><td>"+usd(m.t)+"</td><td>"+usd0(m.p)+"</td></tr>";
      }).join("");
      function set(m){
        mode=m;
        document.getElementById("b-full").setAttribute("aria-pressed",m==="full");
        document.getElementById("b-test").setAttribute("aria-pressed",m==="test");
        draw();
      }
      document.getElementById("b-full").addEventListener("click",function(){set("full");});
      document.getElementById("b-test").addEventListener("click",function(){set("test");});
      draw();
    })();
  })();
</script>
